column9: The eldest or most respected farmer guides communal decisions by consensus.
All family heads hold equal voice on shared concerns. Slower but more egalitarian.
A steward appointed by a distant lord to oversee the settlement. Authority is formal but often resented.
One household head acts as de facto voice for the settlement. No formal appointment, no title. Just the person everyone goes to when something needs deciding.
Simple prayer marker. No resident clergy.
Walk 2-5km to village church for services.

A corner of the holding left out of the plough, banked with turf and marked with fieldstones. No clergy lives near enough to speak over anyone, so the words are said by whoever knew the dead best. The oldest markers have lost their names to the weather and are kept clear anyway.
Somebody in this settlement buys things without asking where they came from. Everyone knows who. Nobody says it directly.
Someone here provides cover for people who need to disappear. A barn, a cellar, an arrangement that isn't discussed.
Wattle-and-daub or timber. 1-2 rooms per household.
Well or spring. 2-4 gallons/person/day minimum.
Sharpened stakes encircling the settlement. Offers minimal protection but enough to deter casual raiders.
One able-bodied adult from each household musters with hunting bows, spears, and farm tools when danger reaches the fields.
A shared underground store for grain, roots, and preserved food. Vital buffer against a bad harvest.
Must travel to manor/village mill. Home grinding often illegal.
Each household farms ~12-16 acres for survival.
Nets, traps, and drying racks. The settlement's economy is inseparable from the water.
Communal flock management. The rhythms of the settlement follow the grazing calendar.
Seasonal felling and timber stacking. The whole settlement smells of fresh sawdust and pine resin.
Repairs tools, shoes horses. Farms also.
Builds/repairs buildings and tools.
A rough landing with racks for drying and salting fish. Primary protein source near water.
Hunters pool knowledge, prepare game, and sell pelts. Tracks routes, seasons, and dangerous animals.
Operates kilns in nearby woodland. Supplies fuel for smithing and baking. Essential intermediate step between forest and forge.
Converts barley into malt for brewing. Small operation supplying local alehouses. Requires grain surplus.
Cuts and dries peat blocks from nearby marshland for domestic fuel. Seasonal. Sells winter warmth.
Communal stable where travelers can leave horses. Stableman provides basic farriery and fodder.
A shallow excavation or shaft dug to extract iron ore, coal, or stone. Employs the poorest labourers. Dangerous, dirty, and essential.
Cuts and dresses stone blocks for construction. A crew of quarrymen with picks and wedges. Slow but the only way to get proper building material.
Buys and sells mules, donkeys, and draft horses. Rents animals to travellers and merchants who need load-carrying capacity for the road.
Keeps cattle or goats for milk, butter, and cheese. The only reliable fat and protein source during grain shortages. Seasonal. Production peaks in summer.
Manages sheep flocks for wool and meat. Seasonal transhumance. Moves flocks between lowland winter pasture and upland summer grazing. Key supplier to the textile trade.
Evaporates naturally saline brine into the raw salt used for preservation. Viable only where salt flats, springs, or other workable brine deposits provide a local supply.
A lord's agent manages the hamlet's lands, collects rents, and enforces noble authority.
A free hamlet with no lord's representative. Communal elder consensus governs shared affairs.
A single respected figure acts as de facto authority. Not elected, not appointed, simply acknowledged. Decisions are practical rather than formal.
Simple prayer location. No clergy.
Travel to village church. 2-5km distance typical.

A walled plot at the edge of the settlement, gated against livestock and kept by the households in turn. The rite is held when a priest comes through, and the burial itself does not wait for one. Families lie in rows by household rather than by standing, which is custom here rather than poverty.
Occasional visits. The smallest spells only.
A rough hall operating under a regional adventurers' charter. Posts bounties, shelters monster hunters, and coordinates local defense when the garrison cannot. Common on dangerous frontiers.
Able-bodied residents drill and muster against local threats. Part-time service.
Basic wooden palisade or earthwork berm. Slows raids and creature incursions.
Stolen goods move through this hamlet quietly. The contact is known by face, not name.
One or more households here have ties to bandit groups operating the surrounding roads. Information, shelter, and supply flow both ways.
Goods pass through here to avoid toll roads or customs checkpoints. The hamlet benefits from fees paid in kind.
Timber-frame with thatched roofs.
Well or spring access.
Home-brewed ale sold from someone's back room. The hamlet's main gathering place. News, disputes, and arrangements all happen here.
A room above a stable and a common meal for travelers passing through. Exists because the road does.

A walled waystation providing secure overnight lodging for merchants, animals, and goods. The centre of desert trade: water, fodder, and protection available for a fee. Without one, caravans cannot safely cross the surrounding terrain.
Monthly or seasonal trading day. No charter. Just habit, proximity, and a flat piece of ground.
Lending against pledged goods. High interest, no questions. The only credit available to peasants and small craftsmen.
Manor mill with milling monopoly (banalité).
Strip farming in open fields.
Shared pasture for village livestock.
Wells and springs throughout village.
Timber construction with stone foundations.
Open-field agriculture with crop rotation.
A single inn serving traders, pilgrims, and travelers passing through. Rooms, stabling, and a common meal.
Local produce and goods. Requires royal/noble charter.
Home-based. Women brew and sell ale.
A flat-bottomed ferry crossing the river. The ferryman's family has held the crossing rights for generations. Essential for anyone who doesn't want a long walk to the nearest bridge.
Builds and repairs flat-bottomed river craft: barges, punts, ferries, fishing boats. Specialist knowledge of river construction: shallow draft, flexible hull, replaceable parts.
An open-air stall or small covered market where the day's catch is sold. Prices drop fast. Fish doesn't wait.
A bridge with a toll house. The keeper collects passage fees and performs basic maintenance. Minor but steady revenue.
A fortified overnight stop with stabling, a well, and basic provisions. Serves merchant caravans and long-distance travellers. Distinct from the inn. Built for animals and loaded wagons, not comfort.
A substantial walled compound for desert merchants: stabling for camels, locked storage, a well, and sleeping quarters for fifty. The economic hub of any desert settlement that sees caravan traffic.
Water or windmill with monopoly milling rights. The miller is often the wealthiest and most resented figure in the village.
Full-time metalworker. Essential for tools and horseshoes.
Builds houses, carts, furniture.
Roof repair and construction.
Makes barrels for storage and transport.

Sells herbal medicines, poultices, and common remedies. Distinct from the alchemist. No magical compounds, no acid flasks. Knows which roots treat fever and which mushrooms kill. Stocked with herbalism supplies.
Makes bows, crossbows, and arrows. Sells finished ammunition and takes custom bow commissions. The first stop for any adventurer whose quiver is empty.
Water- or ox-powered saw. Converts raw logs to planks and beams. Expands construction and furniture output.
A shaft or excavation to extract iron ore, coal, or stone. Requires capital and organisation a thorp cannot sustain, but a village near deposits can. Employs the poorest labourers.
Systematic extraction of building stone. A village on good quarry land can supply half a region's construction needs, and the quarry master knows it.
Operates kilns in the surrounding woodland, supplying fuel for smithing, baking, and heating. The settlement's most reliable fuel source when timber is abundant.
Keeps cattle or goats for milk, butter, and soft cheese. Essential protein and fat during lean grain seasons. Sells surplus at the weekly market.
Evaporation pans or brine processing along the coast or riverbank. Salt is the settlement's most traded commodity by weight. Every household needs it.
Converts hides into leather using oak bark. Foul-smelling. Placed downstream. Essential for shoes, harness, and straps.
Finishes woven cloth by cleaning and thickening it. Often water-powered. Transforms raw weave into durable textile.
Applies colour to raw or woven cloth. Essential for producing anything beyond undyed grey wool.
Wheel-thrown pottery for domestic use. Plates, jugs, storage vessels. Fired in a small kiln.
Moulds and fires clay bricks for construction. Enables more permanent buildings. Requires clay deposits and fuel.
Converts malted grain to ale in quantity. The largest consumer of grain after bread. Supplies alehouses and households.
Maintains stabling, trains horses for riding and draft work. Essential for any settlement on a road.
Maintains hives for honey and beeswax. Honey sweetens; beeswax makes candles, wax seals, and polish.
Buys, salts, and sells fish. The link between fishing and consumption. Near water: fresh. Inland: dried or salted.
Makes and repairs shoes and boots. Every person needs footwear. One of the most reliable and consistent trades.
Cuts and sews finished cloth into garments. Serves the middle tier between home seamstress and master clothier.
Assists with births, manages difficult labours, and provides basic gynecological care. The most-used medical service in any settlement.
Can read and write. Copies letters, draws up simple contracts, reads documents for the illiterate. Often the priest's assistant or a monastery-educated lay person.
Catches waterfowl and game birds using nets, traps, and trained birds. Supplies the market with ducks, geese, and pigeons.
Organises hunting parties across the surrounding territory. Sells venison, pelts, and game to market. Doubles as a source of local wilderness knowledge: which trails are safe, which aren't.
Carves functional and decorative items from wood: tool handles, religious figures, furniture inlays. Produces sacred images and reliquaries for the church.
A craftsman who draws and sells maps: regional road maps, property surveys, and rough wilderness sketches from traveler accounts. Rare enough that most villages don't have one.
Center of village life. Stone construction. Mandatory tithes.
A resident singer, fiddler, or piper. Plays at festivals and weddings. Also a keeper of local history through song.
Performs sacraments, collects tithes. Often only literate person.

Consecrated ground beside the church, on the parish's own plot, with a resident priest to close it. The rite keeps to the day of the death rather than waiting on a clergyman who comes through, and the parish has begun keeping the names in the same book as the baptisms. The ground nearest the church wall is spoken for generations ahead, and everyone here can say who holds it.
A lord's steward collects rents and enforces manor authority over a bound village.
Elected from the peasantry. Organises labour obligations, mediates disputes, and represents the village to outside authority.
The oldest or most respected resident guides village decisions in the absence of formal authority. Less official than a reeve, more stable than nothing.
A resident caster of modest reach. Minor spells only.

A circle of druids tied to the land. They regulate the seasons, mediate disputes with wild creatures, and know which streams run clean. More common in forested or isolated settlements, but they adapt. Some circles tend city gardens or hidden urban groves.
A licensed charter hall providing bounties, monster-hunting coordination, and emergency armed response for the surrounding territory. More common in frontier regions.
Basic healing spells. A closed wound costs 10 in gold.
Organised community defense. Musters for raids and monster incursions. More reliable than hamlet levies.
Perimeter palisade or earthwork berm. Controls approach, slows attackers.
A drinking hall where retired soldiers and mercenaries gather. Informal security, bar brawls, and the occasional job offer for a group needing swords.
Local contact for moving stolen goods quietly. Operates behind another trade.
Goods move through this village avoiding tolls or legal scrutiny. Usually tied to a specific commodity.
Dug smuggling passages beneath the village.
Communal grain storage. Buffers harvests, prevents famine.
Central plaza for weekly markets and fairs. 50-100 yards per side.
Royal charter required. Major economic driver.
Regional merchants. Luxury goods available.
Control trade in specific goods.
Regulate quality, prices, and apprenticeships.
Exchange foreign currency. Early banking (3,000+ population).
Lodging for traveling merchants.
Drinking establishments. Social hubs.
River or coastal dock. Essential for bulk water trade and river transport.
A guild of professional carters, teamsters, and pack-animal drivers who move goods overland for hire. They know every road, every toll, every seasonal closure, and they charge accordingly.
Purpose-built for road travellers: stabling for relay horses, scheduled coach departures, meals served at fixed hours, and a passenger waiting room. Horses changed here, not just rested.
Communal bathing facility with heated water. In some cultures a social hub; in others suspect as a venue for vice. Either way, the best place in the town to hear rumour and news.
A yard where carters, teamsters, and pack-animal drivers can be hired for the road. Returning drivers share road conditions and bandit reports over a cup of ale. Transactional, not institutional.
Constructs and repairs ocean-going merchant vessels. Requires steady timber supply, iron fittings, and specialist shipwright labour. A major employer and a significant capital investment.
Public auction of enslaved persons: war captives, debtors, convicted criminals, and trafficked individuals. Where slavery is legally sanctioned, this is civic commercial infrastructure.

Sells road maps, regional surveys, and coastal charts. Takes commissions for estate surveys and dungeon sketching. Maintains a reference collection of older maps for consultation. Standard stop for adventurers, merchants, and military scouts.
Tests the purity of precious metals brought to the town. Essential infrastructure for banking and minting. Charges fees per assay.
Levies duties on goods entering and leaving via the port or main roads. Run by royal or municipal officials.
Maintains a team of horses for rapid message relay. Letters and small packages travel far faster than foot traffic. Requires coaching inn.
Concentrated stabling, horse trading, and farriery. Serves merchants, military, and travelers needing fresh mounts.

Coordinates regional caravan assembly, departure schedules, and route intelligence. Merchants register goods, hire guards, and arrange joint ventures here. The town-scale predecessor to the city's Caravan masters' exchange.
Works precious metals and gemstones into rings, necklaces, seals, and luxury items. Accepts commissions, appraises stones, and occasionally buys stolen goods from discreet customers.
Produces and ages wine, either from local grapes or imported must. Sells in bulk to taverns and directly to wealthy clients. A vintner in a non-wine region is an importer-blender.

A licensed house that pays for road news and keeps the register: who arrived, from where, and what they carried word of. Cheap to run and openly taxed, which is why it appears wherever traffic does and nowhere that it does not.
Multiple mills for grain, fulling cloth.
Multiple smiths with specializations.
Construction and furniture makers.
Cloth production. Often guild-organized.
Leather production. Foul-smelling; sited by water and toward the settlement edge where the ground allows.
Meat processing. Strictly regulated.
Bread production. Guild-regulated prices.

A proper shop with a trained herbalist, stocked inventory, and a back room for consultations. Sells herbalism kit supplies, common antidotes, medicinal herbs, and basic surgical dressings. Some double as chirurgeons.
Multiple craftsmen organized under a guild. Standard arrows by the sheaf, specialty broadheads, composite bows to commission. Restocks merchant caravans and outfits town militias.
Converts raw ore to refined metal using charcoal-fueled furnaces. The industrial intermediate between mine and smithy.
A water- or ox-powered mill producing planks and beams for the construction trade. A town near timber can supply an entire region's building needs. Employs a permanent crew.
Commercial-scale ale and beer production. Supplies the town's taverns and regional distribution. Major grain consumer and employer.
Full-scale tannery with multiple vats and a guild-trained workforce. Produces high-quality leather for shoes, armour, and saddlery.
Organised shoemakers producing boots, shoes, and sandals for the urban population. Strictly regulated quality.
Master clothiers producing garments from finished cloth. Produces everything from working clothes to livery.
Makes candles from tallow and beeswax. Also produces soap and rope from similar raw materials. Essential for lighting.
Small-scale glasswork: bottles, window panes, goblets. Requires silica sand, potash, and a skilled furnace operator.
Converts refined precious metal into standardised coinage. Requires noble or royal charter. Significant revenue for the granting authority.
Official announcer who reads proclamations, market prices, and news at fixed times in the market square. Employed by the town or a guild.
Twists fibres (hemp, flax, or plant matter) into rope and cordage. Essential for ships, construction, and agriculture.
Multiple parishes within town.
Religious community. May operate hospital/school.
Care for sick poor. Usually religious-run.

Charitable house for the destitute poor, aged, and disabled who cannot work. Funded by church endowment and wealthy donors. Residents receive food and shelter; in return they pray for their benefactors.

Each parish keeps its own ground beside its church, and a parish that has filled its ground buries beyond the gate instead. The sexton holds the register of who lies where, which is the town's longest unbroken record and the one it reaches for in an inheritance dispute. Guilds buy plots together so their members lie among their trade.
Elected or appointed town leadership.
Guilds control town politics. The guildmasters sit on the council.
A lord's appointed official governs; noble authority supersedes local custom.
An informal council of prominent citizens manages town affairs in the absence of formal authority. Less accountable than an elected council, more stable than nothing.
Stone fortifications with gates. Expensive to build and maintain.
All able-bodied citizens obligated to defend town. Part-time service. Present only when no professional watch exists.
Part-time guards. Night patrol and gate duty.
Controlled entry points with gatekeepers.
Housing for guards or small garrison.

A billet and contracting office for a band of professional soldiers available between campaigns. Offers caravan escort, garrison contracts, and short-term military hire at day-wage rates. Cheaper than a standing army, more reliable than a mob. These men fight in formation on salary, not for treasure.
Individual wizard residence. 1,000+ population viable.

A council of senior druids who govern their circle's relationship with the city. They may maintain a hidden grove beneath the streets, mediate between urban expansion and wild places, or serve as ecological advisors to the ruling authority. Found in cities that have made peace with nature magic.
Potions, alchemical items. Basic healing potions (50 in gold).
A ranger station or druid waypost. They monitor the surrounding wilderness, maintain trails, and keep tabs on beast migrations. In times of crisis they serve as emergency scouts and trackers.
Rare permanent circle. Extremely expensive to construct and maintain. Requires magical expertise beyond typical town resources.
Warehouse facilities for merchants storing goods awaiting sale, transit, or seasonal distribution. Essential infrastructure for any trade route settlement.
Job board for torchbearers (1 in gold a session), porters (5 in gold a session).
A chartered hall serving as the primary adventuring hub for the region. Posts contracts, grades monster threats, maintains gear, and coordinates large-scale operations that militia cannot handle.
Non-magical 'divination' using Deception. 1-5 in gold.
Common animals only. Horses, dogs, falcons.
Organized pickpockets and thugs. 10-30 members.
Illicit goods trade. Tax evasion.
Legitimate covers for criminal activity.
A dug network of smuggling tunnels and cellars.

A loft of message birds kept by people who file no returns. Word arrives unsigned and ahead of the watch. Only a standing criminal organization can protect a loft like this, so one never appears without that backing.
Bards, jugglers, acrobats visit during fairs.
Dice, cards, simple games of chance.
Trains fighters for public spectacle. Recruits from prisoners, debtors, and volunteers. Feeds the arena circuit.
Individual or small groups of professional fighters available for private contracts: bodyguard work, debt enforcement, or quiet removal of problems.
Tolerated or regulated prostitution.
Meeting place and administrative center.
Borough court for local justice.
Holding cells and public punishment.
Multi-story timber and stone buildings.
Wells, fountains, or piped water.
Multiple large grain stores distribute food across the city. State managed.
Multiple permanent market squares serve different districts.
Permanent market activity in multiple locations.
Multiple inn districts catering to merchants, travelers, and long-term visitors.
International merchants. Letters of credit accepted.
Loans, currency exchange, letters of credit. Basic banking (5,000+).
Powerful political force.
Extreme specialization (gold-beaters, mirror-makers).
Storage for merchant goods.
If coastal or river access. Essential for bulk trade.
Operates a fleet of river barges on scheduled and commissioned runs. Carries bulk cargo, passengers, and military supply along the river network.
The city-scale version: permanent offices where caravan masters, merchants, and armed escorts transact. Bonded freight, route intelligence, armed convoy assembly, and commercial dispute resolution.
City-scale shipyard constructing large merchant and war vessels. Multiple dry docks, ropewalk, sail loft, and dedicated ironworks. A major employer and a strategic military asset.
Established auction block with holding facilities, registered brokers, and provenance documentation. Legally sanctioned commerce in persons: taxed, regulated, and embedded in the city economy.

A permanent, licensed district for commerce in persons: auction halls, holding compounds, broker offices, and associated legal and financial infrastructure. Operates at a scale beyond a single market block.

A guild of professional cartographers producing regional maps, sea charts, property surveys, and military reconnaissance maps. Sells off-the-shelf maps and takes commissions. The city's maps are the most accurate in the region.

Multiple apothecary shops clustered together. Competition drives specialization. Some focus on chirurgery, others on herbal preparations, others on imported medicines. Herbalism kits, medicinal herbs, surgical supplies, and basic antidotes all available.
State or noble-chartered coin production. Standardises currency across the region. Significant ongoing revenue via seigniorage.
Formal venue for selling high-value goods: estates, ships, livestock, art, and occasionally persons. Charges buyer's and seller's premiums.
Regulates harbour and river-port traffic, collects anchorage fees, assigns berths, and enforces port law. Navigable-water cities only.
Fur processors, traders, and retailers concentrated in one area. High-value trade. Quality furs are luxury goods.

A licensed house that pays for road news and keeps the register: who arrived, from where, and what they carried word of. Cheap to run and openly taxed, which is why it appears wherever traffic does and nowhere that it does not.

The guild form of the listening house: paid correspondents on several roads, an archive that cross-checks one road against another, and a standing rate for a written answer. Expensive to keep, and the only counter in the city where a claim is graded before it is sold.
Armorers, swordsmiths, jewelers. Separate guilds.
Silks, spices, precious goods.
Books and broadsheets (if technology exists).
Windows, vessels, mirrors. Requires expertise.
Bishop's seat. Requires 10,000+ population minimum. Defines major city status.
Different religious orders.
Large facility for sick poor. 50-100 beds.

Receives abandoned infants and young children, providing basic care until they can be apprenticed, placed with families, or raised within the institution. Usually church-run. The wheel in the wall allows anonymous deposit at night.
One per neighborhood.

The parish grounds inside the walls filled generations ago, so the dead are lifted once their term is up and their bones stacked in the charnel house to make room for the next. New ground has been bought outside the gates, and the carts that go out at dusk are a fixed part of the city's evening. Who is lifted and who is left where they lie is settled by what a family endowed.
Elected civic council with full administrative apparatus.
A consortium of guild masters holds effective civic power.
A royal or ducal appointee governs; the city operates as a noble fief.
Wealthy merchant families hold exclusive civic power; political office is effectively purchased.
The settlement governs itself and its surrounding territory as an independent polity. No higher lord, no external charter.
A citizen assembly holds formal authority; eligible voters debate and vote on major ordinances and appointments.
A royal governor or viceroy administers directly on behalf of the crown. High status, high scrutiny.
An administrative apparatus of officials, clerks, and ward officers manages city affairs. Less formally constituted than a council but functional. Governance by bureaucratic inertia.
Masonry walls with towers. Multiple gatehouses.
Full-time law enforcement. ~1% of population.
Professional soldiers. Noble or royal.
Inner fortress. Last refuge in siege.
High-level spellcaster residence. Multiple towers possible.
Organization of magic users. 2,000-5,000 population for chapter.
Multiple alchemical workshops. Guild organization.
Magic item creation. 5,000+ population typically.
Spell scrolls for sale. 25 in gold for the smallest charm, 500 and up for a greater working.
Permanent teleportation circle. Access is controlled and expensive to maintain. Transformative infrastructure for any settlement lucky enough to have one.
Organized crime chapter. 10,000+ population for viable operation. 30-100 members.
Competing gangs. Turf disputes.
Illicit goods trade. Hidden locations.
An extensive warren of smuggling tunnels beneath the city.
An individual or small cell operating beneath the assassins guild threshold. Accepts contracts through criminal intermediaries. Less reliable but deniable.
Warehouses, taverns, shops as criminal covers.

Targets free persons for fraudulent insertion into slavery through forged provenance documents. Where no lawful market exists to absorb the traffic, it runs its own holding, its own escorts, and its own silence.

Fully clandestine operation moving persons across jurisdictions outside legal channels. Only fires where no legal slave market exists. Distinct logistics, safe houses, and corrupt border infrastructure.
Organized contraband trade.

A loft of message birds kept by people who file no returns. Word arrives unsigned and ahead of the watch. Only a standing criminal organization can protect a loft like this, so one never appears without that backing.

The covert guild form: brokers who buy and sell knowledge by the piece, grade what they sell, and will manufacture a claim for a patron who pays enough. It sites itself where the talk already is, among the fences, the late houses, and the inns that ask nothing.
Permanent performance venues.
Dedicated establishments. Some illegal.
Legal or tolerated prostitution quarter.
Illegal or semi-legal combat. Underground locations.
Permanent venues. Professional companies.
Gladiatorial games or monster fights. Massive scale.
Large organized prostitution quarter.
Concentrated gaming houses. Play kept honest by compelled truth.
High culture. Elite patronage.
Formal musical education. Amphitheater, dormitories. 10,000+ for small campus.
Competing organizations.
Organized sellsword companies. Major forces (hundreds to thousands).
Specialized adventuring gear. Warded weapons, silver weapons, etc.
Multiple scholars and researchers.
Goods from other planes of existence.
Ancient wyrm living in city.
Constructed servants if magic permits.
Animated corpses working. Controversial.
Dream-walking magic sold as experience. Lucid shared dreams, communication.
Mooring towers with magical weather protection.
Paired Speaking Stones set in a network. 250-10,000 in gold per station.
Impressive civic building.
Commercial, criminal, and ecclesiastical courts.
Debtors, criminals, political prisoners.

The able-bodied poor receive shelter and food in exchange for compulsory labour: textile work, grinding, construction. Not a prison but the line is blurry. Reduces vagrancy and produces goods. Conditions are deliberately harsh to discourage dependency.
Underground drainage. Rare but critical for health.
Multi-story buildings. Tenements for poor.
Engineered water supply. Conduits, cisterns, fountains.
Over a hundred distinct craft specializations. A guild for every conceivable trade.
Seat of metropolitan or state government: palace, ministries, audience halls, administrative bureaux.
Specialized courts (commercial, criminal, appellate, ecclesiastical) operating simultaneously.
Layered wall systems: outer wall, inner wall, citadel ring. Multiple garrison zones and gatehouses.
Garrison forces distributed across quarters. No single barracks can secure a metropolis.
Hundreds of parish churches across all districts. The faith is woven into every neighbourhood.
Metropolitan cathedral. Seat of the highest regional religious authority. Pilgrimage destination.
Five to ten major monastic houses: scholarly, contemplative, and charitable functions at scale.
Multiple hospitals and infirmaries across districts. Organized medical care at population scale.

Burial has left the walls entirely: grounds beyond every gate, each with its own road, its own gatekeepers, and a trade in plots that the revenue office watches. The parish registers are copied into a central roll because no parish can any longer say where its own dead are. Wards are assigned to grounds, so a family that moves across the city can find itself divided by the assignment.
Formal institution of arcane learning. Full curriculum, research facilities, visiting scholars.
Quarter inhabited by arcane practitioners: towers, workshops, libraries, reagent merchants.
Largest repository of knowledge in the region: thousands of volumes, map archives, historical records.
Formal diplomatic mission from a planar power. Trade, information, occasional intervention.
Dominant criminal syndicate. Tolerated because the alternative (gang war) is worse.
Permanent underground market: contraband, forged documents, illegal services.
Extensive tunnels and catacombs repurposed as criminal and refugee sanctuary.
Professional contract killing. Operates through cutouts, never acknowledged officially.
Superseded at metropolis scale.
Five to ten permanent specialized market districts: grain, livestock, cloth, metals, exotica.
Dozens of merchant guilds representing every major trade good and route. A formal guild parliament.
Consolidated financial quarter: international banking, letters of credit, currency speculation at scale.
Hub for international merchant representatives, trade arbitration, and commodity exchange.
State-administered granary network holding strategic reserves.
State prison complex: political prisoners, debtors, convicted criminals held separately.
Multiple aqueducts, cisterns, and distributed fountains. City-wide water management at scale.
